title: Average rate on an interval
stem: Let f(x) = x² − 3x. What is the average rate of change of f over the interval [1, 4]?

correct.rationale: f(4) = 16 − 12 = 4 and f(1) = 1 − 3 = −2, so the average rate of change is (4 − (−2))/(4 − 1) = 6/3 = 2.

wrong.rationale: 6 is the change in f, f(4) − f(1) = 4 − (−2) = 6, but it was not divided by the change in x, 4 − 1 = 3; the average rate is 6/3 = 2.
wrong.error_pattern: Omits division by the interval length

wrong.rationale: 5 is the instantaneous rate f′(4) = 2(4) − 3 = 5 at the right endpoint, not the average rate over [1, 4], which is 2.
wrong.error_pattern: Confuses instantaneous rate at an endpoint with average rate

wrong.rationale: −1 is the instantaneous rate f′(1) = 2(1) − 3 = −1 at the left endpoint, not the average rate over [1, 4], which is 2.
wrong.error_pattern: Confuses instantaneous rate at an endpoint with average rate

title: Instantaneous velocity from position
stem: A particle moves along a line so that its position at time t seconds is s(t) = t³ − 6t meters. What is the instantaneous rate of change of its position (its velocity) at t = 2 seconds?

correct.rationale: The instantaneous rate of change is s′(2). Since s′(t) = 3t² − 6, s′(2) = 3(4) − 6 = 6 m/s. This is also the slope of the tangent line to the graph of s at t = 2.

wrong.rationale: −2 is the average rate of change over [0, 2]: (s(2) − s(0))/(2 − 0) = (−4 − 0)/2 = −2. The question asks for the instantaneous rate at t = 2, which is s′(2) = 6.
wrong.error_pattern: Confuses average and instantaneous rate

wrong.rationale: −4 is the position s(2) = 8 − 12 = −4 meters, not a rate of change. The velocity is s′(2) = 6 m/s.
wrong.error_pattern: Reports the function value instead of the derivative

wrong.rationale: 0 comes from differentiating t³ as 3t instead of 3t² (giving 3(2) − 6 = 0). The power rule gives 3t², so s′(2) = 12 − 6 = 6.
wrong.error_pattern: Power rule applied incorrectly (exponent lowered but not multiplied correctly)

correct.rationale: This limit is the definition of f′(9) for f(x) = √x, since f(9 + h) − f(9) = √(9 + h) − 3. Because f′(x) = 1/(2√x), f′(9) = 1/(2·3) = 1/6.

wrong.rationale: 1/3 comes from using the derivative of √x as 1/√x, forgetting the factor 1/2. The correct derivative is 1/(2√x), so the limit is 1/(2·3) = 1/6.
wrong.error_pattern: Drops the 1/2 factor in the derivative of √x

wrong.rationale: 6 comes from inverting the derivative, 2√9 = 6. The derivative of √x at 9 is 1/(2√9) = 1/6, not its reciprocal.
wrong.error_pattern: Inverts the power-rule result for √x

wrong.rationale: Substituting h = 0 gives 0/0, which is indeterminate rather than 0. The limit is the derivative of √x at x = 9, namely 1/6.
wrong.error_pattern: Treats 0/0 as 0 after direct substitution

title: Estimate derivative from table
stem:
Selected values of a differentiable function f are given in the table.

x:    0   2    5    6
f(x): 3   7   16   18

Using the two table values closest to x = 4 on either side, what is the best estimate of f′(4)?

correct.rationale: The closest table values on either side of x = 4 are x = 2 and x = 5, so f′(4) ≈ (f(5) − f(2))/(5 − 2) = (16 − 7)/3 = 3.

wrong.rationale: 9 is the change f(5) − f(2) = 16 − 7 = 9, but the slope requires dividing by 5 − 2 = 3, giving 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Omits division by the change in x

wrong.rationale: 2 is the slope over [5, 6], (18 − 16)/(6 − 5) = 2. That interval does not contain x = 4; the closest points on either side are x = 2 and x = 5, giving 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Uses an interval that does not bracket x = 4

wrong.rationale: 9/7 divides f(5) − f(2) = 9 by 5 + 2 = 7. The change in x is 5 − 2 = 3, so the estimate is 9/3 = 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Adds the x-values instead of subtracting

title: Differentiability at a corner
stem: Let f(x) = x² for x ≤ 2, and f(x) = 3x − 2 for x > 2. Which statement about f at x = 2 is true?

correct.text: f is continuous at x = 2 but not differentiable there.
correct.rationale: Both pieces equal 4 at x = 2 (2² = 4 and 3(2) − 2 = 4), so f is continuous. The left slope is 2x = 4 while the right slope is 3, so the one-sided derivatives differ and f′(2) does not exist.

wrong.text: f is differentiable at x = 2 because f is continuous there.
wrong.rationale: f is continuous at 2, but continuity does not imply differentiability. The one-sided slopes are 4 (left) and 3 (right), so f′(2) does not exist.
wrong.error_pattern: Assumes continuity implies differentiability

wrong.text: f is differentiable at x = 2 because each piece is a polynomial.
wrong.rationale: Each piece is differentiable on its own domain, but at the join the left derivative is 4 and the right derivative is 3. They are unequal, so f is not differentiable at 2.
wrong.error_pattern: Checks each piece but not the one-sided derivatives at the join

wrong.text: f is not continuous at x = 2 because the slopes of the pieces differ.
wrong.rationale: Continuity concerns function values, not slopes. The left limit is 4, the right limit is 4, and f(2) = 4, so f is continuous at 2; the differing slopes only prevent differentiability.
wrong.error_pattern: Confuses slope mismatch with discontinuity

title: Power rule with negative exponent
stem: If f(x) = 3/x², which of the following is f′(x)?

wrong.rationale: This loses the negative sign from the exponent −2. The power rule gives 3(−2)x⁻³ = −6/x³.
wrong.error_pattern: Sign error on the negative exponent

wrong.rationale: This adds 1 to the exponent (−2 + 1 = −1) instead of subtracting 1. The new exponent is −3, so f′(x) = −6/x³.
wrong.error_pattern: Adds 1 to the exponent instead of subtracting

wrong.rationale: This lowers the exponent to −3 but never multiplies by the exponent −2. The power rule gives 3(−2)x⁻³ = −6/x³.
wrong.error_pattern: Forgets to multiply by the exponent

title: Horizontal tangent with fractional powers
stem: For x > 0, let f(x) = x^(3/2) − 12x^(1/2). At what value of x does the graph of f have a horizontal tangent line?

wrong.rationale: This uses the derivative of 12x^(1/2) as 12x^(−1/2) (missing the factor 1/2). Then (3/2)√x = 12/√x gives x = 8, but the correct term is 6x^(−1/2), which gives x = 4.
wrong.error_pattern: Drops the 1/2 in the derivative of x^(1/2)

wrong.rationale: This differentiates x^(3/2) as x^(1/2) (missing the factor 3/2). Then √x = 6/√x gives x = 6, but the correct first term is (3/2)x^(1/2), which gives x = 4.
wrong.error_pattern: Drops the 3/2 in the derivative of x^(3/2)

wrong.rationale: This solves f(x) = 0 (x^(3/2) = 12x^(1/2) gives x = 12) rather than f′(x) = 0. A horizontal tangent requires f′(x) = 0, which gives x = 4.
wrong.error_pattern: Sets f(x) = 0 instead of f′(x) = 0

title: Constant multiple and difference rule
stem: Let f be a differentiable function with f′(2) = 4, and let g(x) = 2f(x) − 3x. What is g′(2)?

wrong.rationale: This differentiates 3x as 3x, giving 2(4) − 3(2) = 2. The derivative of 3x is the constant 3, so g′(2) = 8 − 3 = 5.
wrong.error_pattern: Does not differentiate the linear term

wrong.rationale: This drops the constant multiple 2 on f, giving 4 − 3 = 1. The constant multiple rule gives 2f′(2) = 8, so g′(2) = 8 − 3 = 5.
wrong.error_pattern: Drops the constant multiple

wrong.rationale: This adds instead of subtracting, 2(4) + 3 = 11. The difference rule gives 2f′(2) − 3 = 5.
wrong.error_pattern: Sign error on the difference rule

title: Derivative of e^x and cos x
stem: If f(x) = 4e^x − 2cos x, what is f′(π/2)?

wrong.rationale: This uses (cos x)′ = sin x instead of −sin x. The correct derivative is 4e^x − 2(−sin x) = 4e^x + 2sin x, giving 4e^(π/2) + 2.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong sign for derivative of cos x

wrong.rationale: This uses (cos x)′ = −cos x, so the cosine term becomes +2cos(π/2) = 0. The derivative of cos x is −sin x, so that term contributes +2sin(π/2) = 2 and f′(π/2) = 4e^(π/2) + 2.
wrong.error_pattern: Uses −cos x as the derivative of cos x

wrong.rationale: This applies the power rule to e^x as if the exponent were the variable, 4·(π/2)·e^(π/2 − 1). The derivative of e^x is e^x, so the first term is 4e^(π/2).
wrong.error_pattern: Applies the power rule to e^x

title: Derivative with ln x and a reciprocal
stem: Let g(x) = 5 ln x − 2/x for x > 0. What is g′(2)?

wrong.rationale: This uses −2/x² for the derivative of −2/x, giving 5/2 − 2/4 = 2. But d/dx(−2x⁻¹) = +2x⁻², so the term is +2/4 and g′(2) = 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Sign error differentiating the reciprocal term

wrong.rationale: This differentiates −2x⁻¹ as +2x⁻¹ without lowering the exponent, giving 5/2 + 2/2 = 7/2. The power rule gives +2x⁻² = 2/4 at x = 2, so g′(2) = 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Does not lower the exponent in the power rule

wrong.rationale: This differentiates 5 ln x correctly as 5/x = 5/2 but treats −2/x as having derivative 0. The second term contributes +2/x² = 1/2, so g′(2) = 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Omits the derivative of the second term

wrong.rationale: This multiplies the derivatives of the factors, (2x)(3) = 12 at x = 2. The product rule is u′v + uv′ = 31, not u′v′.
wrong.error_pattern: Differentiates a product as the product of the derivatives

wrong.rationale: This keeps only u′v = 4·4 = 16 and omits the second term uv′ = 5·3 = 15. The product rule requires both terms, so f′(2) = 31.
wrong.error_pattern: Omits one term of the product rule

wrong.rationale: This subtracts the terms, u′v − uv′ = 16 − 15 = 1, which is a quotient-rule-style sign. The product rule adds them: 16 + 15 = 31.
wrong.error_pattern: Subtracts the terms of the product rule

title: Identify product rule error
stem: Let h(x) = x²·f(x), where f(3) = 2 and f′(3) = −1. A student writes h′(3) = (2·3)(−1) = −6. Which statement correctly identifies the student's error and gives the correct value of h′(3)?

correct.text: The student multiplied the derivatives of the factors; the product rule gives h′(3) = 2·3·2 + 9·(−1) = 3.
correct.rationale: h′(x) = 2x·f(x) + x²·f′(x), so h′(3) = 6·2 + 9·(−1) = 12 − 9 = 3. The student computed (x²)′·f′ = 6·(−1), which is not the product rule.

wrong.text: The student made only a sign error; the correct value is h′(3) = 6.
wrong.rationale: The error is not a sign slip: −6 is (x²)′·f′(3), the product of derivatives, which is not the product rule. The correct value is 12 − 9 = 3, not 6.
wrong.error_pattern: Misdiagnoses structural error as a sign error

wrong.text: The student omitted f′ from the work; the correct value is h′(3) = 2·3·2 = 12.
wrong.rationale: The student did use f′(3) = −1. The real error is multiplying the derivatives; the product rule has two terms, 6·2 and 9·(−1), and the second term cannot be dropped, so h′(3) = 12 − 9 = 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Believes only the derivative of the first factor is needed

wrong.text: The student differentiated x² when only f should be differentiated; h′(3) = 9·(−1) = −9.
wrong.rationale: Both factors must be differentiated, with one term for each. The correct value is 6·2 + 9·(−1) = 3, not −9.
wrong.error_pattern: Believes only the unknown function is differentiated

wrong.rationale: This reverses the numerator, (2x + 1) − 2(x − 3) = 7, instead of (low)(d high) − (high)(d low) = 2(x − 3) − (2x + 1) = −7. At x = 4 the correct value is −7.
wrong.error_pattern: Reverses the order of the quotient rule numerator

wrong.rationale: This adds the terms in the numerator, 2(x − 3) + (2x + 1) = 4x − 5 = 11 at x = 4, using a product-rule sign. The quotient rule subtracts, giving −7.
wrong.error_pattern: Adds instead of subtracts in the numerator

wrong.rationale: This divides the derivatives, 2/1 = 2, as if (u/v)′ = u′/v′. The quotient rule gives [u′v − uv′]/v² = −7.
wrong.error_pattern: Differentiates a quotient as the quotient of derivatives

title: Horizontal tangents of a rational function
stem: At which values of x does the graph of y = x/(x² + 4) have a horizontal tangent line?

correct.rationale: y′ = [(x² + 4)(1) − x(2x)]/(x² + 4)² = (4 − x²)/(x² + 4)². Setting the numerator 4 − x² = 0 gives x = ±2.

wrong.rationale: 4 − x² = 0 has two solutions, x = 2 and x = −2; the negative root was dropped. Both give y′ = 0.
wrong.error_pattern: Drops the negative root of x² = 4

wrong.rationale: x = 0 is where y = 0 (the numerator of y), not where y′ = 0. At x = 0, y′ = 4/16 = 1/4, so the tangent is not horizontal.
wrong.error_pattern: Finds zeros of y instead of y′

wrong.text: There are no such values of x.
wrong.rationale: This results from adding the numerator terms, (x² + 4) + 2x² = 3x² + 4, which is never 0. The quotient rule subtracts, giving 4 − x² = 0 at x = ±2, so such points exist.
wrong.error_pattern: Sign error in quotient rule numerator

title: Derivatives of sec x and cot x
stem: If f(x) = sec x + cot x, what is f′(π/4)?

correct.rationale: f′(x) = sec x tan x − csc² x. At π/4: sec = √2, tan = 1, csc² = 2, so f′(π/4) = √2·1 − 2 = √2 − 2.

wrong.rationale: This uses (cot x)′ = +csc² x. The correct derivative is −csc² x, so f′(π/4) = √2 − 2.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong sign for derivative of cot x

wrong.rationale: This uses (sec x)′ = sec² x, giving 2 − 2 = 0. The derivative of sec x is sec x tan x, which equals √2 at π/4, so f′(π/4) = √2 − 2.
wrong.error_pattern: Uses sec² x as the derivative of sec x

wrong.rationale: This uses (sec x)′ = −sec x tan x, a sign pattern borrowed from cos and csc. The derivative of sec x is +sec x tan x, so f′(π/4) = √2 − 2.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong sign for derivative of sec x
